events.text: Your first birthday. The family spreads objects on a mat and waits to see what you grab: it is said to decide your whole life.

effects.log: You grab the sword and refuse to let go. Your father pretends not to be proud.
You grab the brush and paint your own face black. Your grandmother declares you a future scholar.
You grab the coins and put one in your mouth. The whole family laughs: a rich life, then.
You grab the herbs and sniff them seriously. The village healer, who came for the rice cakes, takes note.
You grab the thread. A long life, they say, and tie it round your wrist.

choices.text: Nothing: you crawl off the mat

effects.log: You ignore everything and escape across the room faster than anyone can catch you. Nobody knows what that means.

variants: Your first birthday. Objects are laid out on a mat, and the whole family leans in to see what you will grab: they say it decides a life.

events.text: A wandering fortune teller stops at your door, looks at your face for a long time, and asks for three coins to tell your fate.

effects.log: 'Heaven marked this one,' the old man says, pocketing the coins. It is probably what he says to everyone. Probably.
He leaves muttering. Years later you still wonder what he saw.

events.text: You toddle after a dragonfly and straight into the stream behind the house.

ok.log: You somehow reach the bank on your own. Nobody believes you afterwards.

fail.log: Your mother pulls you out by the collar. You are not allowed near water for a year.

effects.log: You hold on to the reeds and scream until someone comes. A sensible child, they say.

events.text: A travelling martial artist practises in the square. You stand behind him and copy every movement, very seriously.

effects.log: He notices, laughs, and corrects your feet once before he leaves. You practise that stance for months.
'Come back when you are taller,' he says, and ruffles your hair. You measure yourself against the door every morning after.

events.text: On winter nights the old people of the village tell stories: the Heavenly Demon, the Sword Saint, the Poison Queen of the south.

effects.log: You dream of a man who cut a waterfall in half. You wake up swinging your arms.
The old woman goes quiet. 'Some stories are not for children.' That only makes you want it more.
You sleep like a stone. Some children need stories less than blankets.

events.text: An old beggar sits by the market gate. You are holding a steamed bun you were very much looking forward to.

effects.log: He looks at you strangely, then laughs until he coughs. 'Good roots,' he says. You have no idea what he means.

choices.text: Eat it in front of him

effects.log: It is a very good bun. He watches you the whole time, and you feel oddly ashamed.

events.text: Playing hide and seek, you squeeze behind the rice jars in the storehouse and find a mouldy bundle of paper.

effects.log: Little men in strange poses, arrows drawn along their arms. You copy them in the dirt for weeks.
Your father turns pale, then burns it. 'Old debts,' is all he says.

events.text: A bigger child pushes you into the mud in front of everyone.

ok.log: He goes down in the mud too. After that he leaves you alone, and so do his friends.

fail.log: You end up in the mud twice. You do not cry. Everyone notices that.

effects.log: You walk home muddy and furious, and spend the evening thinking up a hundred better answers.

events.text: You cannot sleep. You sit in the yard and count the stars until they start to look like a map.

effects.log: You fall asleep outside. In the morning you remember the shape of the sky exactly.

choices.text: Wake your mother to show her

effects.log: You both get scolded. It is worth it.

events.text: A skinny yellow dog follows you home and will not leave.

effects.log: It sleeps outside your door for the next ten years. Nobody sneaks up on this house again.
It runs. Later you feel bad about it, and never quite know why.

events.text: The summer rains flood the lowland. Your family spends three nights on the roof with the chickens.

effects.log: You remember the brown water for the rest of your life, and your father's arm around you the whole time.

events.text: You learn to walk by chasing a rice cake your grandmother holds just out of reach.

effects.log: Five steps, then a fall, then the rice cake. The whole family claps.

events.text: The temple bell rings at dawn every day. You are the only child who laughs every single time.

effects.log: The monks start ringing it a little more gently. The abbot says nothing, but you see him smile.

events.text: The youngest monk carries you on his back while he sweeps the courtyard, and hums the morning sutra so you fall asleep.

effects.log: By five you know half the sutras by heart, and none of the meanings.
He pretends to be a horse. The abbot pretends not to see. It is the best game in the temple.

events.text: An old woman who sells steamed buns under the bridge saves you the burnt one every morning.

effects.log: She starts saving you a good one. Kindness is an investment, she says.

choices.text: Share it with the smaller children

effects.log: You have almost nothing, and you give half of it away. The older beggars start calling you 'little elder'.

events.text: A market guard chases the street children off the rice stalls. You are the smallest, so you are the last.

ok.log: You squeeze under a cart the guard cannot. The older children cheer you all the way down the alley.

fail.log: He catches you by the collar, looks at your face, and lets you go with a rice cake. Some guards are not that bad.

effects.log: You are carried halfway across the city by a very surprised porter. You find your way back by dinner.
